pos.personaBrief: La Maquina's traits were 'constant possession of the ball' (Casazza) and short passes and combinations (Maggio); Muñoz's 'take the ball, give it to me, a gambeta' and the 'Knights of Anguish' who 'didn't look for the goal' show the ball as the point, not space to counter into.

pro.personaBrief: Frascara's ideal (1940) is Sosa who 'construía lento, delicado, suave' and Zumelsu 'de pase corto', with Carricaberry's 'cortada y shot' framed as the exception; Rossi was an attacking centre-half, and River 'didn't look for the goal' quickly.

est.personaBrief: The front five 'changed positions' with 'dynamism and rotating positions', Pedernera moved from the wing to a withdrawn false-nine role and Loustau came inside to help midfield; Borocotó prizes improvisation over the blackboard and Muñoz calls it 'instinctive'.

lar.personaBrief: In the W-M, Muñoz and Loustau opened the pitch and the gambeta-and-cross was the norm (Carricaberry 'despreció la gambeta y el centro' as the exception), but the stars Moreno and Pedernera dropped into the space in front of the half line, and the play was built from short central combinations.

blo.personaBrief: No pressing evidence exists; the side was attack-minded and 'un tanto descompensado en el aspecto defensivo' (Casazza), with forwards devoted to dribbling and combining rather than defending, in a period W-M without a high press.

mar.personaBrief: The only marking evidence is Yácono, 'Estampilla', praised for man-to-man marking who 'would stick to the player he was marking' and would pick up Mazzola in Wilson's hypothetical, within a man-oriented W-M.

pla.personaBrief: Borocotó's 'mil veces los nuestros, aunque pierdan' and the criollo-vs-British self-definition make style an identity kept whatever the opponent; the play grew out of the players' improvisation, with Peucelle fitting roles (Pedernera) to the talent he had.

res.personaBrief: Borocotó (1931) prefers 'los nuestros, aunque pierdan'; La Maquina were 'Knights of Anguish' who 'didn't look for the goal', won only four titles in seven years and are remembered for 'self-conscious romanticism'.

sis.personaBrief: 'Entre el pizarrón y el baldío... mil veces los nuestros' sets talent and potrero improvisation above the blackboard; Moreno kept playing even when turning up drunk, and Muñoz says the goal 'came by itself' from gambeta.

jog.personaBrief: Chantecler (1928) says the criollo style needs 'pequeños y débiles' players who get by 'con maña', against the European 'grandes y fuertes'; the criollo deceives rather than collides, and Moreno 'played in tails'.

bas.personaBrief: Peucelle brought homegrown players up 'with the system already adopted', Pedernera debuted at 16 and Di Stéfano and Carrizo came through, while the canon celebrates the potrero-formed pibe.

lid.personaBrief: Cesarini earned the players' respect rather than imposing discipline, and Moreno's nightlife and turning up drunk were tolerated, with no team discipline measures described.
